meta.title: Gastroesophageal Junction and Pylorus Distensibility Before and After Sleeve Gastrectomy—pilot Study with EndoFlipTM
meta.abstract:
Graphical Abstract

Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s11695-023-06606-2.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A major drawback of sleeve gastrectomy (SG) is the postoperative development of “de novo” or worsening gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) [–]. GERD is considered a risk factor for long-term complications and decreases the quality of life [–]. The gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) (often also referred to as the lower esophageal sphincter) plays an essential role in the complex pathophysiology of GERD, and a better understanding of the associated anatomical and functions is necessary. To date, the usefulness of an endoscopic functional luminal imaging probe (EndoFlip™) in bariatric patients before and after SG to assess the pathophysiological changes in the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) and pylorus with regard to GERD is poorly described. We hypothesized that SG leads to increased distensibility indices (DI) of the GEJ and the pylorus.

sections.title: Materials and Methods
sections.content: This prospective diagnostic observational study included patients (informed consent, ≥18 years, BMI ≥35 kg/m2, fulfillment of the Swiss Society for the Study of morbid obesity and metabolic disorders guidelines criteria) undergoing elective SG at a tertiary care university hospital. The study was approved by the local ethics committee (BASEC ID 2017-00923). Exclusion criteria were pregnancy or breastfeeding, oral anticoagulant, known bleeding disorder, and contraindication for endoscopic examination. Patients underwent esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD), pH-impedance monitoring, high-resolution manometry, and EndoFlip™ (Crospon Medical Devices, Galway, Ireland). GERD was defined (Lyon Consensus 2018) as distal oesophageal acid (pH<4) exposure time >6% and a total number of reflux episodes >80 (as per pH-impedance monitoring) [] and was differentiated between no, stable, de novo, or resolved status when comparing pre and postoperative data. Bariatric outcomes were reported in accordance with the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) guidelines []. Statistical analysis (categorical by Pearson chi-square test and continuous by Mann–Whitney U test) was performed using SPSS Statistics version 25 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, New York).

sections.title: Results
sections.content:
Between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2018, nine patients (Table ) with complete pre- and postoperative EndoFlip™ data were prospectively enrolled in this pilot study. No relevant hiatal hernias were documented.

sections.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
sections.content:
The post-GERD (pGERD) group (de novo or stable GERD, n=4/9) was compared to the no post-GERD (npGERD) group (resolution of or no GERD, n=3/9). Two patients with insufficient GERD data (one conversion to gastric bypass and one without pH-impedance monitoring) were excluded from further analysis. Neither %EWL (p value=0.229), %TWL (p value=0.857), %EBMIL (p value=0.229), nor delta BMI (p value=0.114) at 1 year were significantly different between pGERD and npGERD.

Preoperatively obtained DI (40 ml) of the GEJ were significantly different between the pGERD group and npGERD group (2.6 mm2/mmHg [1.9–3.5] vs. 0.5 mm2/mmHg [0.5–1.1], p value=0.031) (Tables , and Fig. ). No significant difference in the pyloric DI (40 ml) was found (p value=1.000). Intraoperatively, the DI (40 ml) was not significantly different between pGERD and npGERD for the GEJ (p value=0.248) or for the pylorus (p value=0.564). Postoperatively, the DI of GEJ nor pylorus was not significantly different between groups (p value=0.157, p value=0.724) (Table ).

sections.title: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content:
This is the first prospective study assessing pre-, intra-, and 1-year postoperative changes in the GEJ and the pylorus using EndoFlip™ in SG. To evaluate GERD in SG, EndoFlip™ is a promising device for GEJ assessment to predict postoperative long-term functional outcomes. Normative values are required to improve the interpretation of EndoFlip™ in clinical practice. This study showed a significant difference in the DI (at 40 ml filling) of the GEJ by EndoFlip™ pre- vs. 1 year after SG. Preoperative increased DI of the GEJ is associated with GERD 1 year post-SG.

Our perioperative findings are in line with Reynolds et al. and Greenberg et al. [–] who argued that destructed sling fibers at the angle of His are to be regulated. However, these studies were performed in the operating room before and after stapler administration for the SG. We present the first 1-year postoperative data.

The development of GERD after SG may be a dynamic process []. Several mechanisms have been proposed which may lead to the development and resolution of GERD after SG (reduced gastric compliance, increased gastric pressure, shape of SG incl. preservation of antrum, delayed gastric emptying, pylorospasm, %TWL, hiatal hernia, and GEJ complex) []. However, no significant correlation was found between weight loss and change of GEJ measurements in the respective GERD groups.

Contrary to findings from Desprez et al., our results showed a significant increase in the DI of the pyloric sphincter from pre- to 1 year after SG, which could be associated with accelerated gastric emptying [].

A main limitation is that our study consisted of a patient cohort and was insufficiently powered to allow in-depth analysis for the prediction of GERD after SG. The findings of this pilot study suggesting the usefulness of Endoflip™ to predict GERD after SG needs to be verified in larger studies.

reader_sections.title: Why Reflux After Sleeve Gastrectomy Matters
reader_sections.content: Sleeve gastrectomy is a weight-loss operation that removes most of the stomach and leaves a narrow tube. Its main drawback is acid reflux, known as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Some patients develop reflux for the first time after the operation, and others find that reflux they already had gets worse. Reflux lowers quality of life and raises the risk of long-term complications. The **gastroesophageal junction** (GEJ) plays a large part in it. This is the valve where the oesophagus meets the stomach, and it normally keeps acid down. The pylorus, the valve at the stomach's exit, may also matter.

reader_sections.title: Measuring How Easily the Valves Stretch
reader_sections.content:
The team used EndoFlip, a balloon probe passed down through the mouth that measures how easily a valve stretches open. Its reading is the distensibility index (DI), measured in square millimetres per mmHg:

DI = cross-sectional area of the opening / pressure in the balloon

A higher DI means a looser valve. The authors expected surgery to loosen both the GEJ and the pylorus.

reader_sections.title: Patients and Study Design
reader_sections.content: Nine adults with a BMI of 35 or more were treated at a Swiss university hospital in 2018. Each was measured before surgery, during it and one year later, with the balloon filled to 40 ml. They also had endoscopy, oesophageal pressure testing and pH-impedance monitoring. GERD was defined as acid in the lower oesophagus more than 6% of the time plus more than 80 reflux episodes.

reader_sections.title: Key Results
reader_sections.content:
Main findings:

- The GEJ loosened after surgery. Its median DI rose from 1.4 to 2.9 (p = 0.046).
- The pylorus loosened too, from 6.0 to 13.1 (p = 0.046). This may be linked to faster stomach emptying. An earlier study by Desprez and colleagues did not find this change.
- Seven patients had complete reflux data. The four who had reflux at one year (new or continuing) already had looser GEJs before surgery than the three who did not (median DI 2.6 vs 0.5, p = 0.031). Measurements taken during and after surgery did not separate the two groups.
- Weight loss was similar in both groups.

reader_sections.title: What It Means and What Comes Next
reader_sections.content: Earlier studies measured these valves only in the operating room. This is the first to follow them with EndoFlip for a full year after sleeve gastrectomy. The results suggest that a loose GEJ before surgery may predict reflux afterward. Nine patients are too few to confirm this, and EndoFlip still lacks normal reference values, so larger studies are needed.
